checks.claim: Walther Flemming coined 'mitosis' (Greek for thread) in his 1882 book, from stained salamander cells (aniline dyes, salamander larvae)
Flemming described the stage between divisions (interphase) as a 'resting stage' in 1882
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'interphase was first described by Walther Flemming in 1882 as a resting stage between mitotic divisions'. Wikipedia: interphase 'was formerly called the resting phase'. The word 'interphase' itself is later, but the stem only says he called the stage a resting stage.

checks.claim: Alma Howard and Stephen Pelc used phosphorus-32 in broad bean (Vicia faba) root tips, by autoradiography, tracking labelled nuclei
Radioactive phosphorus is built into new DNA (stem simplification)
checks.note: P-32 also goes into RNA and other molecules; Howard and Pelc removed the non-DNA label by acid digestion. 'Which a cell builds into new DNA' is still true as a simplification.

checks.claim: Key: DNA is copied during part of interphase, before mitosis begins
checks.note: 'DNA replication occurs during a limited period in interphase'.

checks.claim: Wrong: during prophase, as the threads thicken
checks.note: Truly wrong: the genome is duplicated in S phase of interphase.

checks.claim: Wrong: during anaphase
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: at a steady rate all through the cycle
checks.note: Truly wrong: the point of the finding is a 'limited period'.

checks.claim: Context: they named that part the S phase, with gaps G1 and G2 before and after
Context: interphase is about nine tenths of the cycle, as the cell grows and copies its DNA; chromosomes enter mitosis doubled
checks.note: Grokipedia 'approximately 90%'; Wikipedia '90% of its life'.

checks.claim: In metaphase chromosomes line up at the middle; each is two identical sister chromatids, held by spindle fibres from opposite poles
checks.note: Sister kinetochores 'must be attached to opposite spindle poles (bipolar orientation)'.

checks.claim: The cell waits until every chromosome is attached from both ends; a single loose one can keep it waiting
checks.note: 'a single unattached kinetochore can sustain the checkpoint'; Wikipedia: 'Even a single unattached kinetochore can maintain the spindle checkpoint.'

checks.claim: Key: the wait guards against a new cell getting both copies of a chromosome
checks.note: Correct attachment ensures 'each daughter cell receives one copy'; premature separation leads to 'missegregation and aneuploidy'. Grokipedia names 'missegregation of both chromatids' to one pole.

checks.claim: Wrong: a chromosome being split before its DNA is copied
checks.note: Replication is checked at G2/M, before mitosis; by metaphase the DNA is already copied. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: two chromosomes trading pieces of DNA
checks.note: Not what the spindle checkpoint senses. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: a break in the DNA being passed on
checks.note: The spindle checkpoint responds to unattached kinetochores, not DNA damage (DNA damage is the G2/M checkpoint's job). Truly wrong in the stem's situation.

checks.claim: Context: moving on too soon leaves one cell with an extra chromosome and the other short, an error common in tumour cells
checks.note: Aneuploidy is 'the most common characteristic of human solid tumors'.

checks.claim: Context: broken or half-copied DNA is caught by other checks before mitosis; trading pieces belongs to meiosis; in telophase a nucleus forms round each set
checks.note: Acceptable 9th-grade simplification. Strictly, rare mitotic recombination exists, but crossing over as a regular step is meiosis's; not wrong at this level.

checks.claim: An animal cell is pinched in two by a contracting ring of protein fibres (actin and myosin) at its equator
Key: a plant cell (onion root tip) builds a new wall (cell plate) from the centre outward
checks.note: Cell plate 'assembles from the center outward via fusion of Golgi-derived vesicles, guided by the phragmoplast' and fuses with the parental walls. Root-tip studies confirm centrifugal growth (https://rupress.org/jcb/article-lookup/doi/10.1083/jcb.130.6.1345).

checks.claim: Wrong: it pinches in, drawing its wall in
checks.note: Land-plant cells form no contractile ring; turgor would resist furrow ingression. (Some algae furrow, but not an onion root cell.)

checks.claim: Wrong: cracks its old wall and each half seals over
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: buds off a small new cell
checks.note: Truly wrong for a plant root cell.

checks.claim: Context: Golgi sacs gather and fuse into a cell plate that spreads until it meets the old wall; a stiff wall and turgor pressure prevent pinching; cytokinesis leaves two cells with identical nuclei
checks.note: Turgor 'approximately 1 MPa, which would resist furrow ingression'.

checks.claim: Many chemotherapy drugs harm healthy tissue: hair loss and fewer blood cells from the marrow
checks.note: Alopecia in up to 65% on cytotoxic agents; myelosuppression 'a primary dose-limiting complication'.

checks.claim: Key: hair roots and marrow are hit because their cells divide again and again
checks.note: Drugs 'target rapidly dividing cells', including 'bone marrow progenitors'; hair follicles hit by 'interference with mitotic activity'.

checks.claim: Wrong: their cells soak up and store the drug
checks.note: Not the stated mechanism. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: their cells take in the most blood
checks.note: Not the reason. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: their cells no longer obey signals to stop
checks.note: That describes cancer cells, not healthy marrow or follicles. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the drugs stop cells dividing; gut lining renewed every few days
checks.note: Renewal 'every 2-5 days in humans' (3-5 elsewhere on the page).

checks.claim: Context: red blood cells last only about four months
checks.note: About 120 days (115-125).

checks.claim: Context: mitosis serves growth, repair and replacement; most nerve cells and heart muscle cells never divide again once mature
checks.note: G0 'irreversible in post-mitotic cells such as neurons and cardiomyocytes'. 'Most' correctly allows for the few exceptions.

checks.claim: All her cells descend from one fertilised egg; she has trillions of cells
checks.note: The zygote 'can develop into any cell type'; an adult has about 30-37 trillion cells.

checks.claim: Key: each kind of cell puts a different set of its genes to work
checks.note: Each cell type 'expresses a subset of all the genes'; Grokipedia: changes in gene expression 'without modifying the underlying DNA sequence'.

checks.claim: Wrong: each keeps only the genes it needs
checks.note: Gurdon: 'nuclear genes are not necessarily lost or permanently inactivated in the course of cell differentiation'. Truly wrong for nerve and muscle (exceptions such as nematode genome loss or lymphocyte gene rearrangement do not apply).

checks.claim: Wrong: each has its own changes in its genes
checks.note: Differentiation does not modify the DNA sequence. Truly wrong as the reason.

checks.claim: Wrong: each has a different number of chromosomes
checks.note: Truly wrong as the reason. Nitpick only: a skeletal muscle fibre has many nuclei, so the whole fibre holds more chromosomes, but each nucleus has the same set and that is not what makes the cells differ. Optional tightening: 'Each nucleus holds a different number of chromosomes'.

checks.claim: Context: nearly every cell keeps the full set of genes; each kind switches on only some, steered by signals around it
checks.note: 'Extrinsic signals from the microenvironment, such as growth factors, hormones, and mechanical forces'.

checks.claim: Context: August Weismann proposed that cells lose hereditary material as they specialise; Gurdon's frogs showed the genes are kept
checks.note: Progressive reduction of germ plasm in somatic cells was 'the part of Weismann's theory which proved most vulnerable'; 'this idea is wrong in most cases'.

checks.claim: Context: mitosis passes the same chromosomes to every new cell; changes to genes are rare mistakes, not the way cells specialise
checks.note: Differentiation 'almost never involves a change in the DNA sequence itself'. Acceptable simplification.

checks.claim: Gurdon destroyed the egg's nucleus with ultraviolet light
checks.note: 'ultraviolet irradiation to destroy the host nucleus'; ASU: UV 'degraded the nucleus of the egg'.

checks.claim: Donor nucleus from a gut (intestinal epithelium) cell of a feeding tadpole; a few eggs grew into swimming tadpoles; 1962 paper
checks.note: Paper title 'The developmental capacity of nuclei taken from intestinal epithelium cells of feeding tadpoles' (1962). About 1.5% reached adult frogs (Scientific American), so 'a few grew into swimming tadpoles' is true.

checks.claim: Donor tadpoles carried a mutation leaving one nucleolus per nucleus, normal frogs two; the eggs came from normal frogs; the new tadpoles' cells had one
checks.note: 'the nuclei of cells carrying the mutation never have more than one'; donor cells from 'mutant tadpoles that had begun to feed'; adults 'carried the mutant nuclear marker'. Marked donor nuclei went into unmarked recipient eggs (1-nu marker, Fischberg's strain; Grokipedia names the '1-nu nucleolar mutation').

checks.claim: Key: the marker settled the doubt that the egg's own nucleus had built the tadpole
checks.note: Skeptics raised 'incomplete enucleation'; ASU: the marker 'indicated that the donor nucleus, not the egg's own DNA, directed development'.

checks.claim: Wrong: a stray unspecialised cell gave the nucleus
checks.note: A real doubt ('contamination by residual undifferentiated cells') that the marker could not settle, since any cell of the mutant tadpole carries it. Truly wrong as the answer.

checks.claim: Wrong: only a rare few gut nuclei could do it
checks.note: The marker says nothing about how many nuclei could; Gurdon used serial transfer for that. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: the light had harmed the rest of the egg
checks.note: Not what a nuclear marker tests. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a team in Basel later used the nucleus of an antibody-making white blood cell and again got tadpoles
checks.note: 1975, Basel Institute for Immunology: 'transplanted a nucleus from an antibody-producing lymphocyte ... into an enucleated egg and obtained living tadpoles'.

checks.claim: Context: Gurdon shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with Yamanaka for showing mature cells can be reprogrammed
checks.note: 'for the discovery that mature cells can be reprogrammed to become pluripotent'.

checks.claim: Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi put 24 genes active in embryonic stem cells into mouse fibroblasts; a very few cells were reset to pluripotent stem cells; published 2006
checks.note: 'twenty-four genes previously identified as important in ESCs'; Cell, August 2006 ('Induction of pluripotent stem cells from mouse embryonic and adult fibroblast cultures by defined factors'); efficiency 0.01-0.1%. Grokipedia: Cell, 25 August 2006; iPS cells 'capable of developing into any cell type'.

checks.claim: They ran the test leaving out one of the 24 each time, and some withdrawals gave no reset cells
checks.note: The paper names 10 factors 'whose individual withdrawal from the bulk transduction pool resulted in no colony formation 10 days after transduction'. Minor wording point: the leave-one-out tests are in the same 2006 paper; 'a result they published in 2006. The two then ran the test...' could be read as later work. Optional: 'The two ran the test again and again...' without 'then', or 'in the same study'.

checks.claim: Key: when leaving a gene out meant no cell was reset, the reset could not happen without it
checks.note: The four were 'each necessary and together sufficient'. Correct necessity logic for the test as run.

checks.claim: Wrong: the reset could happen with it alone
checks.note: No colonies formed when single factors were introduced alone. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: the reset needed it and none of the others
checks.note: Four factors were needed together. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: nothing, until the gene is tested on its own
checks.note: Leave-one-out does show necessity. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: the tests narrowed the 24 to four, Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, and the four together did the job; the cells are induced pluripotent stem cells
checks.note: Strictly two rounds: withdrawal from the 24 flagged 10, then withdrawal from the 10 and combinations gave the four. 'The tests' (plural) covers both; Wikipedia states it the same way.

checks.claim: Context: c-Myc can drive cancer; a quarter of mice given cells made with it grew tumours; later recipes leave it out at the cost of a slower, rarer reset
checks.note: '25% of mice transplanted with c-myc-induced iPS cells developed lethal teratomas'; without c-Myc 'The process took longer and was not as efficient'.

checks.claim: Hartwell and Weinert X-rayed baker's yeast; normal cells halted before dividing, longer for more damage
checks.note: Weinert and Hartwell, Science 241:317-322 (1988): cells 'irradiated with x-rays either arrest or delay cell division' in G2, delaying 'for a time proportional to the extent of damage'. (The stem gives no year; the 1989 paper is the later checkpoint review.)

checks.claim: rad9 mutants did not halt, kept dividing for a few generations and died
checks.note: 'continue to divide for several generations and die'.

checks.claim: Held for several hours with a drug that blocks division, rad9 cells mended their DNA
checks.note: 'efficient DNA repair can occur in irradiated rad9 cells' if 'blocked for several hours in G2 by treatment with a microtubule poison'.

checks.claim: Key: RAD9's job is making the cell wait until the damage is mended
checks.note: 'the RAD9 gene product is essential for arrest of cell division induced by DNA damage'; the response holds cells in G2 until damage is repaired.

checks.claim: Wrong: mending the breaks
checks.note: Ruled out by the experiment: repair was efficient without RAD9 when the cells were held. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: shielding the DNA from X-rays
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: pushing the cell on to its next division
checks.note: The opposite of what the mutants show. Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: Hartwell called such controls checkpoints
checks.note: Checkpoint concept proposed in the late 1980s ('Checkpoints: Controls That Ensure the Order of Cell Cycle Events', Science 1989, with Weinert).

checks.claim: Context: 'he shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Paul Nurse and Tim Hunt, who found cyclins'
checks.note: The relative clause reads as crediting both men with cyclins. Tim Hunt found cyclins (sea urchin embryos, Woods Hole, 1982; https://grokipedia.com/page/Tim_Hunt); Paul Nurse found cdc2, the kinase (CDK) that drives the cycle, in fission yeast, and its human match CDK1. Fix: 'he shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Paul Nurse, who found the enzyme that drives a cell through its cycle, and Tim Hunt, who found cyclins, proteins that build up through each cycle and are destroyed at every division.' (Or drop Nurse's discovery: 'with Paul Nurse and with Tim Hunt; Hunt found cyclins, ...').

checks.claim: Context: cyclins build up through each cycle and are destroyed at every division
checks.note: Accumulated 'progressively between divisions' and almost completely broken down at the start of each mitosis.

checks.claim: Context: a human cell whose checkpoints fail can go on dividing with damaged DNA, a step toward cancer
checks.note: 'defects in checkpoint mechanisms could underlie the genomic instability characteristic of tumor cells'.

checks.claim: Normal cells in a dish divide until they cover the bottom in a single layer, then stop though food remains
checks.note: Normal cells 'formed orderly monolayers and halted division upon reaching confluence'; Wikipedia: arrest 'regardless of external factors or cellular metabolism' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_inhibition).

checks.claim: Key: cancer cells usually go on dividing and pile up in heaps
checks.note: Malignant cells 'pile up in disordered multilayers', 'multilayered foci'; Wikipedia: 'Cancerous cells typically lose this property and thus divide and grow over each other'. 'Usually' in the stem correctly allows for exceptions.

checks.claim: Wrong: stop at a single layer but reach it sooner
checks.note: Typical cancer cells do not stop at the monolayer. Truly wrong for 'usually'.

checks.claim: Wrong: stop short, leaving bare patches
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: die off as soon as they touch
checks.note: Truly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: cancer is cell division that no longer stops when it should; cancer cells often divide quickly, but what marks them out is not stopping when there are enough; in the body this piles cells into a tumour
checks.note: 'Unlike normal cells, cancer cells don't stop growing and dividing when there are enough of them'; they 'often reproduce very quickly'; the build-up forms a tumour. 'Which is what a cancer is' leaves out invasion, but it is the standard 9th-grade definition and not wrong at that level.

unit_notes: One error: cfa6b4cf1a context credits Paul Nurse with cyclins (Hunt found cyclins; Nurse found the CDK kinase). Everything else checks out; optional wording points are noted on b5bfda8682 (muscle fibres have many nuclei) and 22a84d98fe (the leave-one-out tests are in the same 2006 paper, and ran in two rounds, 24 to 10 to 4). Reproduction and embryo-ethics check: no question touches human reproduction or the embryo debate. b5bfda8682 says a girl's cells descend 'from a single fertilised egg', a developmental fact with no reproduction detail; 22a84d98fe names mouse embryonic stem cells only as the source of the 24 genes; 197b11b883 uses frog eggs. Nothing raises the embryo-research ethics question.
